Title: How I use AI (Oct 2026)

URL Source: https://ben.stolovitz.com/posts/how-use-ai-oct-2026/

Published Time: 2026-10-31T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
Wow, things have changed.

[Last October](https://ben.stolovitz.com/posts/how_use_ai_oct_2025), I took stock of how I was using AI — specifically the cool stuff like LLMs that we _call_ 'AI’. I’m so glad I did. Things are very, very different 12 months later.

## [Background](https://ben.stolovitz.com/posts/how-use-ai-oct-2026/#background)

I still believe I use AI fairly typically, but I’ve had a notable change in background. Last October, I was an engineer on Microsoft’s Windows AI team. I am now a research engineer at Salesforce AI Research. I spend more time supporting scientists & building rapid prototypes, rather than working with a large team of engineers. I spend about ~$3,000/​month in tokens.

In any case, I mostly use AI in the same ways as last year:

*   Coding
*   Research & search
*   Summarization & transcription & (new) voice
*   Writing
*   Art & music & (new) video

Also new this year, I’ve drafted a personal **AI policy**; we’ll start there.

As before, this remains purely my opinion & speculation. If you use AI differently, let me know!

## [My AI policy](https://ben.stolovitz.com/posts/how-use-ai-oct-2026/#my-ai-policy)

This year I began drafting a personal AI policy — as in, a document for how _I_ want to use AI in my life. I am very excited about it. I am also working on an explicit AI policy for this site (still thinkin’; probably based on [Hank Green’s policy](https://www.hankgreen.com/ai-policy/)), but a personal policy is to give me a framework for using these tools day-to-day.

AI leaks into life. Teammates ask Claude to write their Slack messages, grandparents generate creepy memes of their grandchildren, and researchers delegate their thinking to machines. I’ve seen all of these things; even strong creators like [Hank Green](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ssE1rmt3EpE) and [BrainPOP](https://x.com/brainpop/status/2102857266584281519) get lost.

BrainPOP using AI art, [perhaps unknowingly](https://x.com/brainpop/status/2102857266584281519)

Humans clearly do not have norms for using these tools, and we’re messing up. I hope that a personal policy will ground me as AI becomes smarter. I hope to adapt that policy over time, and I’m eager to see how it evolves. I’m also open to draft 1 being utterly, hopelessly wrong.

Ultimately, I want to spend my life making cool things with other people. AI can help, AI can hurt. A policy helps me find the difference.

## [Coding](https://ben.stolovitz.com/posts/how-use-ai-oct-2026/#coding)

Writing code is solved.

Last year, I waxed poetic about how GitHub Copilot **autocomplete** transformed how I write code.

Autocomplete is still good (the dim lines)

Well, uh, I no longer write much code. **Agentic coding** has made it obsolete.

My workday now means managing ~5–6 Claude Code (or OpenCode or Codex or Pi) agents. I’ll give Claude a feature to implement, or a bug to reproduce, or any other task I used to do by hand; each agent gets its own copy of the code (a Git worktree, if you’re technical), then just… gets to work. The agents write code, run tests, even create & review PRs.

Claude Code [adds noise-reduction](https://github.com/citelao/mumbo/commit/a92fd3117bde8cf0fa8e323aaa64093eb4466396) to (a worktree of) my Mumble client with one prompt

They are nothing short of magic:

*   They _let me build fast_: agents will prototype any new feature in ~20 minutes. I truly cannot count the number of features, bugfixes, tests, and tools I’ve (AI’ve?) been able to build because of these agents. For example, AI let me test confusing audio code on [macOS](https://github.com/citelao/mac-native-echo-cancellation)_and_[iOS](https://github.com/citelao/ios-native-echo-cancellation) in just a few minutes.

*   They _let me try crazy things_: human teams aim to [“fail fast”](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fail_fast_(business)); agents can fail _ultra_-fast. I’m happy to test crazy new ideas and throw out what doesn’t work well. It was able to wire & test [a huge change to Mumble](https://github.com/mumble-voip/mumble/pull/7180) that added better noise cancelling; I use my beta build of it nearly every day.

*   They _remove drudgery_: I’ve had agents diagnose & fix urgent bugs with nothing more than a description and a “please fix!” while I continued working on other things.

*   They let me _be kinder_: since agents write everything, it is simple to propose sweeping changes to my teammates during code review, or even write my own versions — both things unthinkable in the era of hand-written code.

I do not believe _engineering_ is solved: left to run on their own, agents will build poorly-functioning, over-architected, unreadable, self-congratulatory piles of slop. Every friend I’ve asked agrees that agents _still_ need human taste and experience to produce good work. Some of that is minutiae (like that annoying  status dot  Claude likes to throw onto sites), but most of it is critical. Agents tend to get lost on their own. My most successful work this year was hand-writing a tool, replacing ~4,000 lines of vibe-code with a few hundred. My system has proven more flexible, easier to test, and more generalizable than what it replaced.

It remains to be seen how long that human edge will last, though.

I also now reckon with the _fatigue_ of using these agents. Managing 6 different conversations with 6 different robots about 6 different features is overstimulating & exhausting in a way that coding never was. When I started using agents, I remember rushing to answer their questions like they were human colleagues waiting for help! While I have tempered that [anthropomorphic bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropomorphism#:~:text=people%20use%20their%20schemas%20about%20other%20humans%20as%20a%20basis%20for%20inferring%20the%20properties%20of%20non%2Dhuman%20entities%20in%20order%20to%20make%20efficient%20judgements%20about%20the%20environment%2C%20even%20if%20those%20inferences%20are%20not%20always%20accurate), it’s exhausting to juggle so many problems at once. The allure of sending just one more prompt before lunch… then dinner… oy. There is also, as I wrote in [Consider the chairmaker](https://ben.stolovitz.com/posts/consider-the-chairmaker), the decline of craft. My friend Peter laments ceding the joy of programming to machines: for many of us, honing the code, finding the right design, seeing the parts mesh together — that was the meditative purpose we found in our jobs. Now, we rarely write anything. We instead delegate it to agent number 7.

But let me return to the joy of working with agents: they are so fast, so open to feedback, and so intelligent. Working with them can be utterly delightful.

For example, while I was building a harness for voice agents, one programming agent decided (correctly) that my simple test harness was insufficient. So it used my Mac’s built-in text-to-speech to _directly test the voice agent it was building_. Then, newer agents started doing it, too. Either they had documented the technique, or they were each smart enough to independently discover it. Directly testing the product they were building. Absolutely brilliant.

Agents frequently recommend knobs & settings that I’ll reject for being too complex and unnecessary — and, voilà, I’ll need the knob next week. Silly human!

Anyway, because of agentic coding, **agentic pull requests** are increasingly the way I review agent code. “Make a draft PR,” I write, “I’ll review it soon!” And review it I do — agents still aren’t reliable enough to trust without validating, so I’ll still review their code & test it manually. However, I don’t do the “line-by-line” code reviews I used to do with humans. I focus instead on architecture, on larger patterns in the code. Are there systemic issues with an approach? Should I add new agent guidance to CLAUDE.md? Can I build better test harnesses, so the machines can test their own code?

Agentic **code review** is surprisingly helpful here: I try to write rules for the code review robots whenever I notice a recurring issue with generated code, so the agents will identify & fix issues by themselves. One rule I enjoyed creating: a "[Claude-y comment detector](https://github.com/citelao/dotfiles/blob/main/dotfiles/.chezmoitemplates/skills/claudy-comment-detector/SKILL.md)." You think my writing is verbose? Try Claude’s.

On more typical engineering teams, human code review seems increasingly difficult. A friend of mine complained that his teammates simply ask “their” Claudes to review code written by other Claudes. An ouroboros of Claudes! Agents catch bugs & stylistic issues very well, but they are abysmal at designing architecture. Agentic code review is certainly not a replacement for humans yet.

AI code review [catches](https://github.com/mumble-voip/mumble/pull/7136#discussion_r2972225192) a correctness issue in my code

Last year, I was skeptical of **inline editing** and **code mode**, both features of GitHub Copilot. They were not very useful then, and they are even less useful with agents. I have removed them from the table.

|  | Usefulness | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Autocomplete** | 👍👍 | Still great, obsolete |
| **Agent mode** | 👍👍👍 | The most important use of AI today |
| **Agentic PRs** | 😒 | Validation loop still slow |
| **Code review** | 👍 | Removes some drudgery, but not human-level yet |

## [Research & search](https://ben.stolovitz.com/posts/how-use-ai-oct-2026/#research--search)

Last year, I was excited about research & search: they were the most frequent reason I used ChatGPT. Now, generative AI is the _default_ way I do those things.

The biggest change has been Google’s AI summary. Google’s first or second result is almost always an AI summary, and it’s usually decent. So my **traditional search** is now AI-first by default. Is it perfect? Absolutely not. In one day, it gave me [incorrect URLs for NPR’s RSS feeds](https://www.google.com/search?q=npr+rss) and [couldn’t find the origin of “AI’ve”](https://www.google.com/search?q=ai%27ve+as+a+term+for+thing+made+my+ai&nfpr=1).

But none of the top results clearly gave me NPR’s RSS feeds either, and even Claude [couldn’t find “AI’ve”](https://claude.ai/share/9839381c-f319-41b4-86e2-890bcf89243d). Meanwhile, searching [“HP Reverb G2”](https://www.google.com/search?q=HP+Reverb+G2) gave me the specs I was looking for, [“ai intelligence is spiky”](https://www.google.com/search?q=ai+intelligence+is+spiky) pointed me to the correct term (“jagged”), [“emoji sigh”](https://www.google.com/search?q=emoji+sigh) gave me the right emoji without sending me to [a scummy site](https://emojiterra.com/face-exhaling/), and [“rel nofollow markdown”](https://www.google.com/search?q=rel+nofollow+markdown) reminded me how to link that site without giving them search engine juice.

Before & after: finding emoji online

**Product search** is still mediocre. I’ll _look_ at the summary when I search [“best hysa”](https://www.google.com/search?q=best+hysa), but I don’t trust Gemini to have good advice on where to put my money. Claude certainly helped me [explore budget VR options](https://claude.ai/share/e0f6a055-89a4-418d-97e1-3d924bc57ff7) and understand technical details about [grease for KitchenAid mixers](https://claude.ai/share/9854282b-a5cd-453c-82b9-5977088339db), but can I trust its [coffee table](https://claude.ai/share/eceabd9f-9be0-4aaa-bbc0-4c2e18a51dd1) recommendations? [Sleeper sofas](https://claude.ai/share/0ea61a73-5291-4055-860b-8321a8302b9c)? Let’s not even mention how uncomfortable it is to [see ads in my ChatGPT chats](https://openai.com/index/new-chatgpt-ads-format-and-measurement/).

This ad in ChatGPT isn’t even relevant! And it’s still creepy.

Title: AI Is Changing How Semiconductor Fabs Work — and Engineers Are Moving Faster Because of It

URL Source: https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/ai-semiconductor-fabs/

Published Time: 2026-11-03T16:00:45+00:00

Markdown Content:
Demand for advanced chips is rising. The processes to build them are getting more complex. And the margin for error is shrinking.

For engineers, understanding how a process change will behave, how a material will interact with a new step, how a defect maps back to a root cause are critical, challenging steps in semiconductor manufacturing — and these analyses can take days. Physical experiments on a fab line are slow and expensive. A wrong call on yield or process quality has real consequences.

AI is transforming semiconductor manufacturing, impacting what engineers can do — and how fast.

Accelerated computing shortens simulation time, allowing engineers to evaluate more alternatives before committing to physical trials.

Physics-based AI helps engineers predict process behavior without running a full simulation every time.

AI agents handle sequences of engineering tasks that once consumed hours.

And [digital twins](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/glossary/digital-twin/) let teams test changes in a virtual environment before committing to physical trials.

Together, these capabilities describe an AI-defined fab: a [semiconductor](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/industries/semiconductor/) manufacturing factory where AI helps engineers optimize processes, catch problems earlier and make better decisions across the full manufacturing chip lifecycle. Engineers direct the work and make decisions based on their expertise while spending less time waiting for answers.

## **Shorter Simulation Cycles Change What Engineers Can Explore**

Accelerated computing doesn’t just speed up individual calculations — it changes how many alternatives engineers can test before committing.

Multiphysics simulations model interactions among physical effects, such as heat transfer, electrical behavior and mechanical stress.

Using the [NVIDIA cuDSS](https://developer.nvidia.com/cudss) library, multiphysics software provider [COMSOL](https://www.comsol.com/blogs/accelerating-semiconductor-manufacturing-simulation-with-nvidia-cudss) is accelerating such simulations for semiconductor manufacturing by up to 10x. This helps engineers optimize equipment and processes, compare alternatives and decide which changes to test physically.

Applied Materials and NVIDIA are collaborating to accelerate atomic-scale materials discovery and process development. By integrating NVIDIA cuDSS, Applied’s Ginestra simulation platform runs up to 10x faster than CPU-only approaches. And with NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo, Applied’s ACE+ multiphysics platform delivers topography simulations up to 35x faster.

In some cases, acceleration doesn’t just shorten the calculation — it enables it altogether. Computational lithography — which defines how circuit patterns are printed onto silicon — involves calculations too intensive to complete on CPU at production scale. Siemens is integrating[NVIDIA cuLitho](https://developer.nvidia.com/culitho) into its Calibre lithography software, delivering up to 17x acceleration on key simulation workloads. That expands what engineers can verify before a wafer goes to print.

As such, faster calculations can help researchers explore material behavior and reaction pathways that influence next-generation semiconductor processes.

## **Predicting Process Behavior Without Running Every Simulation**

In addition to accelerating simulations, AI trained on physics can predict how materials and processes will behave — without running a full simulation each time.

The payoff is most visible in complex calculations that are expensive even on accelerated hardware.

Plasma — the electrically charged gas used in semiconductor etch processes — is one example. Modeling plasma behavior requires solving equations that capture how electrical, chemical and thermal processes interact, making repeated simulation costly. Lam Research demonstrated that the[NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo](https://developer.nvidia.com/physicsnemo) framework can predict plasma behavior in milliseconds, compared with days for a full simulation — giving engineers a faster way to explore process conditions without rerunning the full model each time.

Applied Materials uses digital twins built on NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to simulate fab-level optimizations in layout, throughput, cost and process control.

## **Agents Handle the Steps Between Decisions**

Engineers turn analyses into decisions — revising a design, investigating a test failure, adjusting a production process and more.

AI agents can help carry out the steps between those decisions.

Evaluating which AI model to apply to a given task is one example: a sequential, manual process that can consume hours on the test floor.

Advantest is using [NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/route-ai-agent-workloads-across-models-with-nvidia-nemo-switchyard/) AI agents to automate that selection, reducing response times from hours to minutes.

## **Testing Factory Changes Before They Reach the Line**

Digital twins let teams simulate equipment configurations, layouts and process changes in a virtual environment before committing to physical trials. This reduces experimentation costs, especially as fabs become more complex and the stakes of a wrong change get higher.

A photorealistic fab digital twin built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries, used to simulate material flow, spot bottlenecks and validate operational strategies before deployment. Image courtesy of Applied Materials.

[Applied Materials](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/advancing-semiconductor-innovation-across-materials-engineering-and-manufacturing/) uses[NVIDIA Omniverse libraries](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/omniverse/) to build physically accurate digital twins of entire fabs. Teams can simulate material movement, identify bottlenecks and evaluate layouts and operating strategies — extending virtual experimentation beyond individual processes to how the factory works as a whole.

## **The Connected Loop**

The future of semiconductor manufacturing lies in connecting these capabilities: using production data to inform models and models to evaluate changes, then bringing those findings back to the engineers making production decisions.

That’s the promise of the AI-defined fab: where AI helps people learn from each production cycle and act on that knowledge sooner.

_Explore how_[_NVIDIA is working with semiconductor leaders_](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/industries/semiconductor/)_across the chip lifecycle._

Kairos is open-source, real-time fraud and risk decisioning
Kairos
decides every sign-up, login, order, payment and payout as it happens, and keeps each decision with the signals behind it. It is an open-source alternative to Sardine, Sift, Riskified and SEON, with two things they don't have:
your coding agent tunes it
, and
decision models
catch fraud before you have the labels to train on.
Decisioning
Real-time decisions
: one call returns approve, step up, review or block, with a risk score and the reasons, from the subject's history, the devices, cards and addresses it shares with others, and the session.
Workflows
: ask a decision model, score with a model, branch, call webhooks, open cases, and decide again later.
Queues and cases
: review work for people, whose resolutions become labels.
Agent-first
MCP server
: Claude Code, Cursor or Codex read your decisions and build workflows, with every action recorded under its key.
Experiments
: your agent proposes model variants, Kairos trains and tests them on your data, and the agent ships the winner.
Decision models and traditional ML
Grayson
: Finic's decision model answers questions about each request in plain language. It works with few labels and reads unstructured data.
Models
: logistic regression and gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost-compatible) on your numbers and Grayson's answers, trained in Kairos or uploaded.
For developers
SDKs
for TypeScript (
@finic-ai/kairos
) and Python (
finic-kairos
), a
CLI
, an
HTTP API
, and
self-hosting
with Docker.
An AI fraud ML engineer, always tuning on your data
You send Kairos what happens in your product: sign-ups, logins, orders, payouts, chargebacks. It decides each request (approve, step up, review or block) and keeps every decision with the signals behind it.
What makes Kairos different is who tunes it. Connect Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or any agent over
MCP
, and the agent can do the work of a fraud ML engineer:
Build the workflow.
It defines what to decide, which questions to ask a decision model, and which fields to score.
Design experiments.
It proposes variants: a decision model alone, logistic regression on your numbers, gradient-boosted trees, a stack of them, or the decision model's answers combined with your numbers in one model.
Let Kairos run them.
The server trains each variant on your oldest labeled data, chooses on the next, and tests on the newest, then reports ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, the gain over a baseline with its 95% interval, and precision and recall at your thresholds.
Pick the winner and ship it.
The agent explains its choice, applies the variant as the workflow's next version, and comes back when new labels arrive.
You:     "Our chargebacks went up. Find a better model for shopify_order and publish it if it wins."
Agent:   designs six variants → create_workflow_experiment → reads the results →
         "Logistic regression on the order's numbers plus Grayson's answers wins: ROC-AUC 0.949 on validation,
          0.930 on test. Publishing it as v6."
Decision models and traditional ML, together
Kairos is built around
Grayson
, Finic's decision model. You ask it questions in plain language ("Does the shipping address look like a reshipper?", "Is this email throwaway?") and it answers with calibrated probabilities. Decision models are strong where traditional ML is weak:
Few labels.
Grayson works on day one, before you have the thousands of chargebacks a model needs to learn from.
Unstructured data.
It reads descriptions, emails, names, addresses, notes and item titles, which a gradient-boosted tree can't.
Explanations.
Every answer is a question you wrote, so every decision says why.
Traditional models are strong where decision models are weak: they learn your own outcomes precisely, from your own numbers, and they cost nothing per decision. Kairos lets you combine both: Grayson's answers become features next to your fields in a
logistic regression
or
gradient-boosted trees
(XGBoost-compatible, trained in Kairos itself), and experiments tell you which combination wins on your data.

Jay Peters
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.
Many indie game developers have recently posted on social media about unexpectedly long approval wait times for their game submissions on Steam, with some of the approvals causing developers to miss their planned launch dates.
For example, Studio Daimon, the team behind an upcoming title called
Food Devils
, had planned to launch the game in early access today after submitting its build on October 12th. But the game is “still awaiting approval,” according to
a post from game director Alfred Kamon
. “Even now, we don’t know when Steam will give us the final OK to finally release our game. We sent another ticket last week saying that the situation was urgent and that we might miss our release date because of this,
but it also got ignored
.”
In October, publisher 2 Left Thumbs
said it missed
its planned launch of
Wheel Make It
“by nearly two weeks” due to the long wait for build reviews. You can read some details about the studio’s setbacks, including failing a review for a “one single option in the menu” not being accessible with a controller,
in a Steam post
. There are
lots
of
other
recent
posts
about review build waits as well.
Valve says on
a Steam developer website
that a review of a game’s store presence “typically takes 3-5 business days to complete,” though the company suggests submitting a page for review “at least 7 business days before you want it live to account for potential changes you’ll need to make.”
However, as of late, Steam has seemingly been grappling with a sharp increase in games; October’s Steam Next Fest had 7,240 games, a 65.2 percent increase over June’s Steam Next Fest,
according to
How to Market a Game
. A Reddit user
also found
that 49.9 percent of all games released since Valve started asking developers
in 2024
to label games that use AI now have an AI disclosure.
Kamon
and
2 Left Thumbs
suspect the longer waits are due to “slop” slowing down the process. “We can only assume it’s because Steam’s review queue is clogged up by AI slop, but the whole process is now taking several weeks for some developers,” said Kamon.
In a
new post from Valve
published after we first ran this story, the company acknowledged that following a “a significant increase in submissions for store and page review in recent months,” it’s “running a little behind right now” and taking “up to 12 business days” for reviews, saying that much of the delay is “having to re-review games.” It has updated its release checklist for developers, including requiring them to run a game through Steam for at least five minutes. Valve also says that further improvements are on the way for the build review process.
Itch.io has also been dealing with a rise in games, with the platform
saying last weekend
that “The number of game pages being created per-day has doubled in the past 2 months.” Last night, the platform
said it
“Just deleted a couple terabytes of ai slop 😌”

articles.content:
Title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too

URL Source: https://simonwillison.net/2026/Nov/3/qwen-can-interpret-model-weights/

Markdown Content:
3rd November 2026

Yesterday’s hot paper was [Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights](https://rikiyat.github.io/blog/weight-space-programming/) by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a “blog post”, but it’s paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model—literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I’ve been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I’m delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well!

#### Weight-Space Programming

Here’s the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term **Weight-Space Programming** for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights:

> Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra **can tell what a network was trained to do**. And without any environment feedback, it **has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks** that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.
>
>
> Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra **identifies an issue in its weights** causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own [model card](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B/blob/main/README.md#L856) warns about, and **fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights**. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.
>
>
> All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this **Weight-Space Programming**.

The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights _without_ running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models.

spaCy author Matthew Honnibal [called the paper misleading](https://honnibal.dev/blog/astra-read-write-misleading) for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke [deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example](https://www.seangoedecke.com/llms-are-not-superhuman-at-reading-and-writing-neural-network-weights/) as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use.

I’m going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two.

The paper presents the first question as **Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights?** They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games—Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had [to look that one up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freeway_(video_game)), it’s an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question:

> `The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response.`

The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is [RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs](https://github.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs). The [exp1_which_game](https://github.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/tree/main/exp1_which_game) folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games:

I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others.

#### Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models

The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My [LLM](https://llm.datasette.io/) tool has a `-f/--fragment` option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this:

llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \
  -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro

This example requires the [llm-openrouter plugin](https://github.com/simonw/llm-openrouter) installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here’s [what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro](https://gist.github.com/simonw/9f18d2945a105c04734ef7e5cd95717c), which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens.

But how about [Qwen 3.8 27B](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Aug/16/qwen-38-27b/)? That’s still my favorite model to run on my own laptop—it’s just 17GB (I use [this version](https://huggingface.co/lmstudio-community/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF/blob/main/Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf)) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025.

I fired up [LM Studio](https://lmstudio.ai/), ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the [llm-lmstudio](https://github.com/llm-lmstudio/llm-lmstudio) plugin and ran this command:

LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \
  llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \
  -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b

(I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see [this issue](https://github.com/llm-lmstudio/llm-lmstudio/issues/16).)

After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop [returned a response](https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2F387d3a7927f165b1986bb6c2099d0f53#response-1) that ended like this (here’s [the reasoning trace](https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2F387d3a7927f165b1986bb6c2099d0f53#reasoning-1)):

> Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets.
>
>
> Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards.
>
>
> Confidence: 72%

This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It [identified Pong](https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2F387d3a7927f165b1986bb6c2099d0f53#response-2) ([reasoning](https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2F387d3a7927f165b1986bb6c2099d0f53#reasoning-2)) in 1h 4m 54s:

> **Pong** — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object.
>
>
> Description:
>
>
> The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized.
>
>
> Confidence:
>
>
> **75%**

And [Breakout](https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2F387d3a7927f165b1986bb6c2099d0f53#response) ([reasoning](https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2F387d3a7927f165b1986bb6c2099d0f53#reasoning)) in 52m 25s:

> Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game.
>
>
> Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty.
>
>
> Confidence: 88%

Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn’t surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here’s [that transcript](https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2F6ed68f659e26a32e7d9096391d92f326)—Qwen thought it was “A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally”.

The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here’s a sample:

> What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let’s list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right?

That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort.

It’s a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I’ve seen around it does not feel justified. I’m not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways.

The biggest modding site in PC gaming is taking a stance on AI
Nexus Mods says that authors of newly uploaded mods will have to declare whether AI was ‘used in their work.’
Nexus Mods says that authors of newly uploaded mods will have to declare whether AI was ‘used in their work.’
by
Jay Peters
Nov 4, 2026, 12:42 AM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Image: The Verge
Jay Peters
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.
The PC gaming mods repository Nexus Mods is making disclosures about AI mandatory for uploads of new mods, meaning that mod authors will have to declare “whether AI has been used in their work,” the site
announced today
as part of a big post about AI-generated content on the platform.
“One of the most consistent concerns we’ve heard is that it’s not clearly disclosed when AI has been used to create a mod,” according to the post from site owner Victor “Foledinho” Folmann. “We already have tags for AI-generated and AI-assisted mods, but we recognise that there’s a lot more we can do to make that information more accessible and clear for you all.” Any mods tagged as “AI-assisted” will also be required to include “a public explanation of how and where AI was used.” AI tags will also be “more prominent” on mod pages.
Folmann says Nexus Mods is “pro-human creativity” but “won’t introduce an outright ban on AI-generated mods.” As for why that is:
The answer is simple: AI is currently used throughout the whole process of creation, from script autocompletion to generation of textures, voices, and full assets, and it is difficult to draw a clear boundary between what is acceptable and unacceptable. An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process but will prevent people from mentioning its use. We’d prefer the opposite; it should be out in the open, clearly labelled, and regulated according to the rules that we can implement on our platform.
Folmann notes that Nexus Mods won’t use mods to train AI and “will not sell or license them to anyone doing so.” However, the site is working on “clearer control” over how mods can be reused on others and strengthening attribution for when “a mod uses another Mod Author’s mod with the appropriate permissions.”
Nexus Mods is also making changes to the Recently Added section of the site to address a problem of mod authors uploading many mods at once, which makes other mods fall down down the page. “This is less of an issue related to AI, but it’s becoming much more prevalent as mod production is speeding up,” Folmann says. The changes include trying limits on how many mods from one author are shown at a time and “tighter restrictions” on uploads from new accounts. The platform is also launching controls to hide AI-generated content in game pages and on the homepage, and “next up,” in search.
Related
Valve is making changes to deal with a ‘significant increase’ in Steam game submissions
Nexus Mods’ full AI policy
is here
, and mod authors have 60 days to update their existing mods to meet the requirements. The 60-day grace period ends on January 2nd, and after that time, the site will begin enforcing the rules.

Starting today, Siri can tune into the Apple Watch’s mic with
Audio Intelligence features
that are available in the new watchOS 27.3 developer beta rolling out now. The two new additions are Siri Recap, which uses “ambient listening” to generate summaries of your conversation, and Live Rewind, which generates text transcripts of the last 15 seconds of audio your watch’s mic detected.
Apple is also
releasing
its
redesigned Health app
for testing today in the iOS 27.3 developer beta, and announced expanded language support in global English, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese. It adds sections like a new Insights tab with summaries for heart, sleep, fitness, and other data that pop up during the day, a For You section with personalized recommendations, and health content like educational videos and articles.
Apple
:
Live Rewind, which can help users recall what was just said in conversation. A double-press of the Digital Crown shows the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as a text snippet, so the user can catch something they may have missed or are less familiar with. Users can ask Siri about the content of the text or save it to the Siri app to revisit later.
Siri Recap, which can create high-level summaries of conversations that users can review later to jog their memory. When Siri Recap is turned on, after a conversation, Apple Intelligence automatically generates a title and key points in the new Siri app, allowing users to be more present and engaged in the moment.
When it comes to the implications of an ambient, always-listening AI, Apple has released
this Audio Intelligence
Privacy Overview (pdf)
about
how it plans to protect users’ privacy
when their watch is listening around the clock. It goes into detail about Apple’s claims that users’ raw audio “is handled within dedicated hardware, is not saved as a file, and is not accessible to the operating system, apps, or Apple.” According to Apple, “If you use iCloud with two-factor authentication and have a device passcode, any Siri Recap summary or Live Rewind text snippet you choose to save syncs across your devices end-to-end encrypted in the Siri app.”

Abstract:
This book provides a compact, derivation-oriented introduction to the mathematical foundations of modern generative artificial intelligence. Rather than surveying every recent architecture or implementation detail, it develops a coherent route through the ideas connecting major families of generative models, from PCA, probabilistic PCA, variational autoencoders, and diffusion models to normalising flows, autoregressive factorisations, GANs, Wasserstein GANs, and energy-based models. The aim is to make the structure of generative modelling more accessible without removing the mathematical substance needed to understand how these models are derived and related. The book is intended as a foundation-building primer for mathematically curious researchers, practitioners, and students.

Those Jeff Bezos hair transplant photos are very fake
In the era of easy AI fakery, edited paparazzi photos are a reminder that not everything is what it seems.
In the era of easy AI fakery, edited paparazzi photos are a reminder that not everything is what it seems.
by
Jess Weatherbed
Nov 3, 2026, 9:01 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
These edits of Jason Statham (left) and Jeff Bezos are a bit jarring, but that’s sort of the point.
Image: The Verge
Jess Weatherbed
is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.
Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and actor Jason Statham have a distinctive feature in common: They’re both famously bald, and that definitely hasn’t changed in the last few days. However, there are
some images
of the two men
circulating around X
,
Threads
, and
Bluesky
in which they both have substantially more hair than their usual shaved look, which in Bezos’ case appears to be
very
freshly transplanted. It’s all just photo editing fakery, AI or otherwise.
It’s unclear
how viral
these
posts are
, but they’re prevalent enough that a few members of the
Verge
team have encountered them in their social media feeds. Some people who shared them claimed (or were seemingly fooled into believing) that Bezos and Statham had undergone hair transplant surgery. Generative AI tools have made this kind of photo manipulation or outright creation more accessible and convincing, and because
AI labeling solutions
on social media
broadly suck
at flagging this fakery, it’s easy to be misled unless you’re wary of
everything
you see online. In a world where social media shitposters can turn engagement into a revenue stream, they’re not going to stop churning out attention-grabbing fabricated nonsense anytime soon.
Related
Nobody is safe from celebrity AI deepfakes
How the experts figure out what’s real in the age of deepfakes
We don’t know if AI tools were used to make the follicled Bezos and Statham edits — none of the images I tested flagged for Content Credentials or SynthID markers. We also can’t fully establish when they were first posted or who made them, but they
are
definitely fake, and it only took me a couple of minutes to confirm it.
In both cases, I ran the photos through Google’s reverse image search tool. For the Bezos debunk, I found photographs of him in a similar background environment and wearing the exact same outfit (with, yes, no hair) that included a watermarked image credit at the bottom left. Searching for the credit then led me to the
original photographs
in their unaltered state, which were taken in 2023. Finding the original tressless images of Statham was even easier — the reverse image search immediately surfaced watermarked versions of the originals, which were
snapped by a paparazzo in 2011
.
Both of the original photos were actually taken on the same day, at around the same time, but anything for clicks, right?
Image: Eliot / Spread / MEGA
There’s other evidence too if you know what to look for. The main flag is that it’s probably impossible for Bezos and Statham to be realistic candidates for hair replacement surgery anyway; it requires you to have enough “donor” hair to sacrifice from the back and sides of your head to then replant closer to your desired hairline. You can
technically
take it from other places (or even other people), but doing so is incredibly rare due to undesirable results and rejection concerns. Transplant patients also typically experience some pretty dramatic facial swelling for the first week or so, which Bezos shows no signs of. Wigs, toupees, and other hair systems can also be used as nonpermanent hair restoration solutions, but as someone who used to make and install them professionally, it would be an
astounding
whoopsie for someone as rich and connected as Bezos to go this route and still end up
looking like a Chia Pet
.
This isn’t the first time photo-manipulated fakery has fooled people across social media, and with ongoing generative AI advancements, it probably won’t be the last. Previous incidents gave us the
viral swagged-out pope
, and recent trends have seen
paparazzi photographs of celebrities
like Callum Turner, Harry Styles, and Noah Schnapp being manipulated to remove their shirts. These kinds of edits are typically designed to rack up likes, reposts, and other engagement — they play into our fascination with celebrities’ lives with fabricated situations that are
just
outlandish enough to be believable, grab our attention, and be shared around as the latest hot gossip by those who are fooled, or who simply don’t care to verify the facts.
If you’re ever unsure if there’s fakery afoot with images of famous faces, just remember that most of the convincing edits (AI or otherwise) are based on real photos that you can hunt down to verify the original source.

Apple starts giving Siri AI access to third-party apps

by

Link

Emma Roth
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.
Apple will now let Siri AI perform actions across third-party apps. As part of the iOS 27.3 update rolling out on Tuesday, Apple
announced developers
can now integrate Siri AI’s new features in “all apps,” allowing the voice assistant to draw on a user’s personal context, process natural language prompts, and use on-screen awareness to complete requests.
The update, which is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview, also adds a new “app skills” feature that third-party developers can create to combine several tasks into a single action. In
Apple’s developer documentation
, the company says users won’t have to mention an app’s name in their request while it’s in the foreground, during a Live Activity, or in a conversation with Siri AI about the app.
“For example, a person might request a ride with a ride share app, follow updates to the app’s Live Activity while they wait for their ride to arrive, then request to move the pickup location to a different address by saying ‘Hey Siri, change my ride pickup to a new address,’” Apple says. As
noted by
9to5Mac
, Apple previously made a smaller set of features available to third-party developers.
Related
Apple is all in on AI — its own and everyone else’s
Siri AI is already changing how I use my iPhone
Apple is bringing Siri AI’s expanded capabilities to its own apps as well, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather apps. “Users can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year,” according to Apple. The company notes that users can ask Siri AI what it can do in each app.

articles.content:
Title: macOS 27 Golden Gate does not actually support CoreStorage volumes – Wade Tregaskis

URL Source: https://wadetregaskis.com/macos-27-golden-gate-does-not-actually-support-corestorage-or-hfs-volumes/

Markdown Content:
macOS 15 Sequoia had a hard time with CoreStorage – and thus encrypted HFS+ volumes – since it deprecated both technologies and callously crippled some important tools for working with them, but nonetheless it _mostly_ still worked. While I’d often – but not always – have to manually unlock one of my HFS+ volumes – but not the others – at boot, and it also refused to convert some – but not all – volumes from HFS+ to APFS[1](https://wadetregaskis.com/macos-27-golden-gate-does-not-actually-support-corestorage-or-hfs-volumes/#c63a9f61-72c1-4689-a06c-d132ac976f25), keeping me trapped in the situation – it ultimately still _worked_. I could get at my data and use the volumes more or less normally.

Unfortunately, in macOS 27 that’s no longer the case. Not only does Golden Gate just not support CoreStorage / encrypted HFS+ volumes, out of the box you can’t do _anything_ with them – can’t mount them, can’t convert them to APFS, can’t even erase them. It renders your expensive storage hardware completely useless.

Worse, macOS 27 puts up a misleading dialog, upon boot, saying that macOS _28_ (the _next_ version) won’t support these volumes. I have no idea what Apple’s doing or thinking. Maybe it’s all just an embarrassing misunderstanding – the file system team told the notifications team that CoreStorage & encrypted HFS+ support is going away, and typoed the version number as 28 rather than 27?

## Details

macOS 27 cannot mount CoreStorage volumes automatically or through any normal means. Worse, Disk Utility can’t mount them even when manually told to – it just fails with the cryptic error:

> com.apple.DiskManagement.disenter error 49,153

`diskutil mount`_also_ fails, this time with an error message that is a blatant lie:

> `disk27 is a CoreStorage Logical Volume which is locked; use "diskutil coreStorage unlockVolume"`

**$ diskutil cs unlockVolume BC304645-7D99-481E-931F-855B3011D89D**BC304645-7D99-481E-931F-855B3011D89D is already unlocked and is attached as disk27
**$ diskutil cs list**CoreStorage logical volume groups (1 found)
|
+-- Logical Volume Group 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB
    =========================================================
    Name:         Smash
    Status:       Online
    Size:         2000054960128 B (2.0 TB)
    Free Space:   0 B (0 B)
    |
    +-< Physical Volume 1B5A1754-184B-4F17-A797-BF69B4BB627F
    |   ----------------------------------------------------
    |   Index:    0
    |   Disk:     disk10s2
    |   Status:   Online
    |   Size:     2000054960128 B (2.0 TB)
    |
    +-> Logical Volume Family 376204CD-8048-4962-B05C-72F4FC16B77B
        ----------------------------------------------------------
        Encryption Type:         AES-XTS
**Encryption Status: Unlocked**        Conversion Status:       Complete
        High Level Queries:      Fully Secure
        |                        Passphrase Required
        |                        Accepts New Users
        |                        Has Visible Users
        |                        Has Volume Key
        |
        +-> Logical Volume BC304645-7D99-481E-931F-855B3011D89D
            ---------------------------------------------------
            Disk:                  disk27
            Status:                Online
            Size (Total):          1999702634496 B (2.0 TB)
            Revertible:            No
            LV Name:               Smash
            Volume Name:           Smash
            Content Hint:          Apple_HFS

Tangentially: surprisingly, [hfsutils](https://www.mars.org/home/rob/proj/hfs/) (installed via [brew](https://brew.sh/)) don’t work at all:

**$ sudo hmount /dev/disk27**hmount: /dev/disk27: not a Macintosh HFS volume (Invalid argument)
**$ sudo hmount /dev/disk10s2**hmount: /dev/disk10s2: not a Macintosh HFS volume (Invalid argument)

But what’s even worse about this dumpster fire is that macOS 27 _can_ mount these volumes just fine – it’s just that all the _normal_ ways to do it are completely broken. If you go down to a lower level and run `mount_hfs` directly, it _does_ work:

**$ sudo mkdir -p /Volumes/Smash
$ sudo mount_hfs -o rdonly /dev/disk27 /Volumes/Smash
$ ls /Volumes/Smash**
Documents           Pictures           Scratch space
That said… that `-o rdonly` parameter… in principle it shouldn’t be required, but I could _not_ get macOS 27 to let me mount any HFS-on-CoreStorage volume as read-write – no matter what I did, it always fails with error “Resource busy” (EBUSY). I spent a lot of time trying to debug this, and could find _no_ evidence of anything having the volume in question open (nothing in `lsof` etc).

But wait, it gets worse.

macOS 27 can’t even erase the volume. All the normal tools – `diskutil`, Disk Utility, etc – fail with that same “Resource busy” error.

## Workaround

Thankfully, with the help of Gemini 4 Argon, I did find a workaround. It’s convoluted, but takes only a few steps, thankfully.

First, while if you try to delete the logical volume group it ostensibly fails, it doesn’t _completely_ fail – it does actually delete the logical volume(s) within:

**$ diskutil cs delete 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB**Started CoreStorage operation
Unmounting Logical Volumes
Destroying Logical Volume Group
Erasing disk10s2
newfs_hfs: cannot create filesystem on /dev/rdisk10s2: Resource busy
Mounting disk
Could not mount disk10s2 after erase
Error: -69832: File system formatter failed
**1 💣 $ diskutil cs list**CoreStorage logical volume groups (1 found)
|
+-- Logical Volume Group 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB
    =========================================================
    Name:         Smash
    Status:       Offline
    Size:         2000054960128 B (2.0 TB)
    Free Space:   -none-
    |
    +-< Physical Volume 1B5A1754-184B-4F17-A797-BF69B4BB627F
        ----------------------------------------------------
        (No properties)
**$ diskutil cs delete 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB**Started CoreStorage operation
Destroying Logical Volume Group
Error: -69783: Unable to delete the CoreStorage Logical Volume Group
You still can’t destroy it completely, nor can you erase the physical volume yet – the “Resource busy” errors persist. But, the trick is to _restart_ – after that, you _can_ then erase the volume.

So it seems that whatever broken thing is holding the physical volume (or logical volume group) in a ‘busy’ state is tied to the existence of the logical volume(s) therein, and once they’re deleted (and the machine rebooted) the bug stops being triggered.

## Call for better workarounds

I’ve glossed over a _lot_ of debugging and attempts I made to save the volume in-place, by either making it work as-is (even if only with e.g. hfsutils) or by converting it to APFS, but neither I nor Gemini 4 Argon could find anything that worked. It’s too late for me – I was forced to just delete all my HFS+ & CoreStorage volumes and rebuild them painstakingly from backups – but if anyone finds a way, I’d love to amend this post, for the benefit of future readers.
